title: Episode 250: Crazy Horse: Tasunke Witko, the Battle of the Rosebud, Custer's Last Stand, and the Unbroken Spirit
description:
The enigmatic and unconquerable life of Tasunke Witko—Crazy Horse: the greatest battlefield commander and mystic warrior of the Oglala Lakota nation. Never allowing a photograph to be taken, refusing to wear war bonnets or scalp locks, Crazy Horse lived entirely according to a sacred childhood vision of a rider passing through hail and bullets untouched. Orchestrating the decoy ambush at the Fetterman Fight, outmaneuvering General George Crook at the Battle of the Rosebud, and leading the decisive charge that broke Custer's Seventh Cavalry at the Little Bighorn, Crazy Horse defended his ancestral lands to his last breath before his tragic assassination at Fort Robinson in 1877. Discover the immortal warrior who never surrendered his spirit.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series chronicles the most mysterious and unconquerable warrior in the history of the North American continent: the Oglala Lakota mystic who refused to be photographed, touched, or tamed. Here is George with the life of Tasunke Witko: Crazy Horse.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE LIGHT-HAIRED BOY AND THE THUNDER VISION: 1840
Born around 1840 near Bear Butte in the Black Hills of modern South Dakota, the boy who would become known as Crazy Horse entered the world during a turbulent era of westward migration and intertribal conflict. Because of his unusually light, wavy brown hair, sandy complexion, and quiet, withdrawn disposition, his family named him 'Cha-O-Ha'—meaning 'In the Wilderness' or 'Curly'. While other Lakota youths were boisterous and competitive, Curly was an introspective, brooding solitary child who loved wandering alone in the pine hills. At age fourteen, following the Grattan Massacre of 1854, in which rash U.S. Army troops slaughtered Chief Conquering Bear's village over a wandering Mormon cow, the traumatized youth sought a vision on a rocky hilltop. For three days without food or water, he lay in prayer until a profound sacred trance overtook him: he saw an unadorned warrior riding a horse through a storm of thunder, lightning, and whistling bullets. The warrior wore no war paint, took no scalps, and carried only a red-tailed hawk feather in his hair and a small brown pebble behind his ear, passing completely untouched through the fire because he thought only of protecting his people. His father, a holy man also named Crazy Horse, interpreted the vision: the rider was Curly himself, and he would be invulnerable in battle as long as he took no trophies, wore no ostentatious ornaments, and never hoarded wealth. To seal the sacred vision, his father bestowed upon him his own name: Tasunke Witko—Crazy Horse. The light-haired youth was guided throughout his life by the solemn memory of his sacred vision, convinced that personal modesty and spiritual purity were his only true shields against the bullet storms of battle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: RED CLOUD'S WAR AND THE DECOY AMBUSH: 1866
In 1866, the United States government constructed the Bozeman Trail through the heart of the Powder River buffalo country to connect the Oregon Trail to the gold fields of Montana, building three military forts along the route in direct violation of Lakota treaties. In response, Oglala Chief Red Cloud launched a relentless guerrilla war to shut down the trail. Crazy Horse, now twenty-six years old, emerged as the peerless tactical genius of the conflict. On December 21, 1866, outside Fort Phil Kearny in Wyoming, Crazy Horse led a small, daring decoy detachment of ten warriors mounted on agile ponies to lure the garrison out. Captain William Fetterman, an arrogant Civil War veteran who had famously boasted that with eighty men he could ride through the entire Sioux nation, took the bait with eighty-one soldiers. Crazy Horse taunted the troops, dismounting to inspect his pony's hoof and dancing in front of their rifles just out of range. Fetterman pursued the decoys over the crest of Lodge Trail Ridge, directly into a massive, concealed ambush of two thousand Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors. In less than thirty minutes, Fetterman and his entire command were annihilated in the snow. It was the worst military defeat the U.S. Army had suffered on the Great Plains up to that time, forcing the federal government to sign the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, abandon all three forts, and close the Bozeman Trail forever. Crazy Horse's tactical brilliance in the Fetterman fight demonstrated a sophisticated mastery of psychological warfare, turning an enemy commander's arrogance into an insurmountable tactical trap.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MYSTIC LEADER WHO REFUSED TO BE SEEN
As Red Cloud and other chiefs settled onto government reservations to receive food rations, Crazy Horse retreated into the pristine wilderness of the Powder River, refusing to accept white civilization. He became an almost mythical, spectral figure: he never allowed his photograph to be taken, believing that capturing a person's image trapped their soul and diminished their power. While other chiefs wore resplendent feathered war bonnets and beaded buckskin shirts, Crazy Horse dressed in simple, unadorned robes, riding a spotted pinto horse with lightning streaks painted across his cheeks and white hailstones dotted on his chest, exactly as seen in his childhood vision. He never bragged about his deeds at the victory fires, never danced in public celebrations, and gave away all horses and buffalo meat captured on hunts to the widows, orphans, and elderly of his camp. His people loved him with passionate devotion because he asked for nothing for himself, embodying the highest Lakota moral ideal of total selflessness in service to the community. Crazy Horse's refusal to sit for a photograph or wear the regalia of an agency chief reflected his deep mystic belief that the spiritual essence of a warrior should belong only to the Great Mystery and his people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BATTLE OF THE ROSEBUD: JUNE 17, 1876
In the spring of 1876, the U.S. Army launched a massive three-pronged offensive to crush the non-reservation Lakota and Cheyenne who refused to cede the Black Hills. General George Crook advanced from the south with over one thousand cavalry, infantry, and allied Crow and Shoshone scouts. On June 17, along the rolling ravines of Rosebud Creek in southern Montana, Crazy Horse demonstrated military generalship of breathtaking brilliance. Instead of fighting in traditional loose tribal bands, Crazy Horse unified fifteen hundred Lakota and Cheyenne warriors under a coordinated tactical command structure, rotating waves of charging horsemen and exploiting the undulating terrain with lightning cavalry maneuvers. For six exhausting hours under a scorching sun, Crazy Horse struck Crook's flanks, broke his battle lines, and forced the battle-hardened general into a humiliating strategic retreat back to his supply base in Wyoming. Crook was entirely knocked out of the campaign, leaving General Custer's Seventh Cavalry advancing alone from the east with no southern support and no inkling of the massive, victorious warrior army waiting just across the Wolf Mountains. At the Battle of the Rosebud, Crazy Horse's innovative coordination of multiple tribal war bands broke the military cohesion of General Crook's veterans, demonstrating field generalship of the highest order.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE WHIRLWIND AT THE LITTLE BIGHORN: JUNE 25, 1876
Eight days after the victory on the Rosebud, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer attacked the great encampment on the Little Bighorn River. When Custer's battalion attempted to cross the river at Medicine Tail Coulee, native fire turned them back onto the high, dry sagebrush ridges. Crazy Horse rallied hundreds of young Oglala and Cheyenne warriors, famously shouting his electrifying war cry: 'Hokahey! It is a good day to fight! It is a good day to die! Strong hearts, follow me!' Instead of attacking Custer's fortified defensive positions head-on, Crazy Horse led his warriors on a sweeping, concealed ride through deep northern ravines, cresting the ridge behind Custer's command and cutting off all avenues of retreat. Sweeping down upon Custer's position like a sudden prairie whirlwind, Crazy Horse's warriors rode directly into the cavalry skirmish lines, firing repeating Winchesters, bows, and war clubs in hand-to-hand combat. In less than an hour, Custer and all two hundred and ten men under his immediate command were dead. Crazy Horse's brilliance on the battlefield that afternoon cemented his reputation as the greatest light cavalry tactician in North American history. The sweeping ride through northern ravines at the Little Bighorn showed Crazy Horse's extraordinary battlefield intuition, striking Custer's rear at the exact psychological moment to shatter cavalry resistance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WINTER OF STARVATION AND SURRENDER: MAY 1877
The victory at the Little Bighorn was the glorious sunset of the Lakota world. In the brutal winter of 1876 and 1877, General Nelson Miles unleashed a ruthless campaign of winter warfare, burning tipis, destroying food stores, and slaughtering remaining buffalo herds in sub-zero blizzards. In January 1877, Crazy Horse fought his final battle against Miles at Wolf Mountain in a blinding snowstorm, his warriors firing their last scarce cartridges. With his people starving, women and children dying of frostbite, and his beloved young wife Black Shawl suffering from advanced tuberculosis, Crazy Horse made the agonizing decision to surrender to save his people from extinction. On May 6, 1877, Crazy Horse led nine hundred proud Oglala followers into Fort Robinson, Nebraska. Thousands of reservation Indians and U.S. soldiers turned out in stunned silence to watch the legendary warrior ride in: wearing no war paint, head bowed in dignity, Crazy Horse laid down his rifle and buffalo robes before Lieutenant William Philo Clark, an unbroken titan who had never suffered defeat in battle. Crazy Horse's surrender at Fort Robinson was born not of personal defeat, but of profound compassion for the starving women, frostbitten children, and wounded elders of his band during a merciless winter campaign.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BETRAYAL AT FORT ROBINSON AND THE UNBROKEN SPIRIT
Crazy Horse's presence at the Red Cloud Agency ignited dangerous jealousy among rival reservation chiefs, who spread false rumors that the great warrior was plotting to assassinate General George Crook and launch a new uprising. When Crazy Horse left the agency without permission to take his sick wife to her parents at Spotted Tail Agency, soldiers arrested him. On September 5, 1877, Crazy Horse was brought under military guard into Fort Robinson. When he realized that the guards were leading him into a dark stone guardhouse with iron bars on the windows, the wild plainsman drew a hidden knife and fought desperately to escape. As his former friend Little Big Man held his arms from behind, a military guard named Private William Gentles lunged forward and plunged a bayonet deep into Crazy Horse's kidneys. The thirty-seven-year-old warrior fell mortally wounded into the dust. Refusing to lie on a white man's cot, he was placed on a blanket on the office floor, where he died late that night with his elderly father singing his death song beside him. His parents took his body into the Black Hills, burying him in a secret mountain canyon that has never been found. Today, his spirit is carved into the granite of Thunderhead Mountain in South Dakota, the largest mountain sculpture in the world. Crazy Horse remains an eternal monument of human liberty: the warrior who could not be bought, bribed, photographed, or broken. The tragic bayoneting of Crazy Horse at Fort Robinson robbed the Plains of its purest warrior, but his legend endures as an unvanquished spirit of freedom, forever riding the sacred winds of the Black Hills. Today, the monumental mountain carving of Crazy Horse in the Black Hills of South Dakota stands as an eternal testament to a Lakota leader who never signed a treaty, never gave up his rifle, and never surrendered his soul.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 253. Until then, stay curious.
